514.t: Segregated Memphis clubs and the dance-blues repertoire
514.s: Clubs were segregated in 1950-52; the repertoire included The Hucklebuck, Night Train and slow blues with vocalists.
514.q: Yes. The clubs were segregated at the time but there were a couple of artists [who] would be able to come in, but for the most part all the clubs were segregated, yeah.

514.t: Little mixing of black and white musicians; playing West Memphis, Arkansas
514.s: Almost no integration, though they played white-owned clubs across the bridge in West Memphis for white audiences.
514.q: Very, very little. Yes. I really can’t call it integrated, no, ‘cause like I said because it was before the total segregation. But what we would do, we could go to places like West Memphis, Arkansas, which was like across the bridge from us, and we would play in the white-owned club for the white…

107.t: Segregated audiences and the white slummers
107.s: The band played to black audiences only, with a few white 'slummers' or music lovers attending.
107.ch: Cincinnati bands, race and the road to college
107.q: We played for black folks. There were no mixed audiences in those days. You either played for all black audiences or all white audiences.

107.t: Racial contact among musicians: the Rhythm Kings and jam sessions
107.s: Foster played a few white dances as the only black member of the Rhythm Kings, and says interracial sitting-in was relaxed; he knew little of Cotton Club jam sessions.
107.ch: Cincinnati bands, race and the road to college
107.q: No, whenever it happened, it was cool. Like there was a band called the Rhythm Kings. They met me through my music teacher that I was going to Wurlitzer, to take lessons. Some of these guys, they became aware of me. They invited me to play with their band. I played at a couple, or maybe more than a…

146.t: Roped-off dances with White and Black sides
146.s: Smith confirms big halls used a rope to separate White and Black dancers.
146.ch: Road life, arranging and racial dangers
146.q: : out there, we had three bands there, and they had a rope right down the middle...

146.t: Segregated dances and carrying a show
146.s: Smith played White and Black places, carrying a dance act and chorus girls in the Black venues; mixed dances became normal later.
146.ch: Dallas bands, Ray Charles and family
146.q: too? We played all of them, White and Black. We go and play for two or three days down there at a White place, and then we'd leave there and go and play at a Black place three or four days. They'd carry a show in there, but they didn't carry no show in the White place. They had me come all around…

76.t: Italian dancers, and the first Black band in a white hall on Pine Street
76.s: White Italian youths from Dago Hill began coming to the Black dance hall and then hired Creath for a white hall on Pine Street, a first for a Black band in segregated St. Louis.
76.ch: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
76.q: And then this was a colored dance hall, but these Italian boys and all around St. Louis started to hear about this jazz and they started to come into this dance hall 'cause they could dance by this music. And boy, we had as many white as blacks. They almost took it over because they loved that…

76.t: The mixed benefit band at the Booker Washington Theatre
76.s: Zutty and Creath invited the white West Lake musicians, including Pee Wee Russell and Bix, to play a benefit at the Booker Washington Theatre; Zutty thinks it was his first mixed band.
76.ch: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
76.q: But I think that was the first mixed band I ever played with because Charlie was going to play this benefit for Bob Russell. He was a Negro producer, you know, and they were giving a big thing at the Booker Washington Theatre. That was right in the section, you know. And so Charlie said to me, said…

172.t: Playing white fraternity dances and Louis Prima
172.s: Ridgley says the band was welcome in white homes and at fraternity dances. Louis Prima came to hear them at a ball park every Sunday.
172.q: We could have had the two bands that had done them all. But we were well light-minded people and everybody tried to have us. We could go anywhere, anybody would have us in the house. We were always dressed well and neat. It was all right to get along with the people and they were very nice to us.…

241.t: Playing dances for white and Italian-sponsored jobs along the river
241.s: He says most work was for white people, with some Italian-sponsored dances and halls for colored patrons.
241.q: So, he, uh, we used to play all through length, you know, and then we used to play elsewhere, you know, for colors, you know. So, uh, played the Wool Forest Hall back at Gratner. The what? Wool Forest. Oh, the Wool Forest.

288.t: Playing Tulane fraternity dances; few white musicians took to jazz early
288.s: Charles says his band was first to play Tulane fraternity dances; white players came later and seldom sat in.
288.ch: Opening and early New Orleans customs
288.q: we were the first one well good then we used to play for those those youngsters too you know yeah they called us fraternity dance we used to play all those fraternity dance back there sure

635.t: Colored bands, white passengers and Monday night rides
635.s: Two Black bands played on one boat, two white bands on the other; Black passengers could come only on Monday nights.
635.q: On Monday nights, the colors used to come on the stairs and say, boys, we have a boat ride every Monday night. But then we played like we want. We had fun, we drank, smoked, we were at hell on Monday night, man. We used to whisper Monday night to come. Yeah. And they used to have a lot of white…

602.t: Playing for white strip shows and the proposed band screen
602.s: At the Moulin Rouge he emceed striptease shows, and a woman tried to require screens in front of Black bands.
602.q: And I remember one time, Miss Wurrlein tried to get them to pass a law that every nightclub had a show and had a black band that had to have a screen in front of the band.

967.t: Playing rural Louisiana towns to mixed audiences
967.s: King describes his gigs in towns like Lafayette and St. Martinville and the question of segregation.
967.ch: Audiences, segregation and rock and roll
967.q: Yeah. Because. Most of my performances. Throughout. Uh. Louisiana. During the year. Was in the rural towns. You know. South Louisiana. Lafayette. St. Martinville. You name it. In that. Locale. And it was. Predominantly. With uh. The whites. And the blacks. But uh. In some locations. You get. Uh.

311.t: Big bands at Sweet's and Thad's Ballroom and audience segregation
311.s: Bands played some nights for white and some for black audiences in Oakland ballrooms until things changed.
311.q: Yes they did. Over at Sweet’s, over there, yeah. It was that way yeah. Yeah they did have that. It Thad’s Ballroom or Sweet’s, I forgot, over in Oakland. Most of the dances were in Oakland, more so than San Francisco. We’d go over there, the first time I heard Lunceford and those bands. And I…

910.t: Segregated dance halls in the South
910.s: At dances with Bostic and Dinah, halls roped off sections by race, and young people cut the ropes to join the music.
910.q: Not down the middle, down the side. They made the nucleus of it for the blacks to dance, and they’d have a rope on the side, and they’d cut the rope. And the kids back then, they’d put up another rope, and after they’d cut the rope and they’d be out. I mean this was all the time. Because that’s…

939.t: Segregated dances and the rope that fell down
939.s: Audiences were divided by a rope or balcony, but dancing would knock the rope down until officials stopped the music.
939.q: Well most times, as I said, we worked warehouses and barns, and nine times out of ten that didn’t have what you call the “second balcony.” If we were lucky to play a county hall or an auditorium sometimes, they had a balcony, and in that balcony was called the spectators. These were the whites who…

692.t: First date at Club Alabam and 'Can Dave Brubeck swing'
692.s: Iola tells of her first date to a San Francisco club where a woman asked if Dave was colored; talk of critics doubting his swing and his different style.
692.q: No, I was not. I knew nothing. I knew nothing about it. However, we were talking last night about an incident when we were with some friends. And they asked about when we were first going together and dating. And Dave said on this first major date we had we went to San Francisco and we went to a…

407.t: Playing the white YMCA and who listened to the music
407.s: The first black band at the white YMCA was told to play 'their people's music'; Carn reflects on white kids' knowledge of black music.
407.q: Well there were a couple of incidents, but nothing that would break the spirit you know. I’ll tell you once we played at the YMCA downtown you know, so we was the first black band quote unquote to play at the white YMCA. And I think this was ’61 you know. And so — maybe ’62. So we played at the…

158.t: Improving conditions, Paul Higaki, and mixed audiences in the South
158.s: Things improve around 1948; he recalls Japanese trombonist Paul Higaki with Hampton and Millinder audiences in San Antonio mixing the segregated chairs.
158.q: This is coming into like 1948. And see then, every now and then up north you could stay in a white hotel. See but it wasn’t still that much, although I have to put in a little thing here. We had a trombone player that played with Lionel Hampton, and he was Japanese, Paul Higaki, and it was worse…

113.t: Segregated audiences kept apart by a rope
113.s: At some dances whites and blacks were on separate sides, divided by a rope.
113.q: Yes. In some places we played I mean whites on this side and blacks on that side you know.

349.t: Youngest in the band and mostly white audiences
349.s: He was the baby of the group, too young to drink, and the audiences were mostly white.
349.ch: Early gigs and the war years
349.q: No, no. And it’s a funny thing that you say that. It would always seem like I was the youngest, the baby in the group. And the guy would say, “No, man, like you don’t —” And it was some time, man, I played out there before I was able to take a drink. The guys would look out, “No, no, no. You’re too…

122.t: Sweet's Ballroom: separate white and colored nights
122.s: Dance halls excluded minorities; Sweet's ran a colored night and a white night with the same band.
122.ch: Big bands in the Bay Area
122.q: In the thirties, the late thirties, even up to the forties before, in Oakland, at Sweet’s Ballroom, that’s where most of the fellas went because that’s where the big bands would make their appearance, the dance halls they had here they were more like steady jobs. They were regular Saturday night…

222.s: Audiences were not integrated; Sweet's Ballroom in Oakland gave Black patrons one night, Monday.
222.q: Right. I remember in Oakland there was a dance hall, a very nice dance hall, it was called Sweet’s Ballroom, all the bands appeared there. But for the Afro-Americans there was only one night and that was a Monday night, and the rest of the nights were for the whites. And that’s how it was in most…

490.t: Race in Detroit and the Blue Bird club
490.s: He says Detroit musicians did not feel segregation, and describes sneaking in to play piano at the Blue Bird before turning twenty-one.
490.q: No, really in Detroit, I’ll be honest with you, we didn’t know nothing about race anyway, see. We didn’t know nothing about this segregation until they told us about integration, ‘cause we were all so mixed up, you know. Um, oh man, I can’t think of names now.

101.s: Black and white boat rides and later segregated dances on the road, including the rope across the bandstand.
101.q: Something like that. Yeah. You could dance and listen to the music. But it too was racial. They had black boat rides and white boat rides. Everything was a two-way in those days. Matter of fact, when I first went on the road down South, we played dances. On certain days it would be for the whites…

86.t: Whites behind the rope at Black dances; Freddie Green made to walk in the street
86.s: He describes tobacco-warehouse dances, segregated crowds and the mistreatment he and Freddie Green faced.
86.q: Well, not only police, civilian harassment, all kind of harassments. You know, it’s a funny thing, I can’t understand it. White people didn’t want to be bothered with us but they’d come to the dance and stand behind the rope and listen to us play. They’d come to the black dances. They would have to…

224.t: Mixed bands and audiences; the Harvard Jazz Society
224.s: Bands and clubs in Boston were mixed; the Harvard Jazz Society brought Bechet, Bunk Johnson and Pops Foster, and Haynes met and played with them.
224.ch: Boston drummers and a first New York trip
224.q: Yeah. I think those were the people that started bring people like Sidney Bechet. They were there a lot. I met Bunk Johnson and – what was the bass player’s name that played with them? From New Orleans . . .

400.t: Cross-racial friendships and the roped dance floor in Greenville
400.s: Hinton recalls Greenville, Mississippi, dances with Cab Calloway where a rope divided the floor, and Taylor mentions the Jewish community there.
400.ch: Eddie South, high school and the South Side scene
400.q: Greenville, Mississippi was an unusual town. I played there with Cab Calloway back in the early days and it was amazing to see the racial relationship there. There were black kids there with blue eyes. I mean my color with blue eyes, which was quite unusual. We would play a dance in Greenville and…

509.t: The Wheel and the first integrated band in Maryland
509.s: She describes a rough bar on Bladensburg Road where her integrated band won over the crowd.
509.q: We worked at a joint called The Wheel. It‘s out on Bladensburg Road, definitely a redneck place. But the drummer knew the owner, and the owner liked my music, so we went out there. It didn‘t make any difference to me. I just wanted to play. They came in; a couple of my girlfriends came in. Both of…

65.t: How the Machito band came to open the Palladium
65.s: The Alma Dance Studios turned Palladium were failing; Machito, asking if the owner was prejudiced, proposed mixing audiences in a segregated era.
65.ch: Mambo, the Palladium and Cubop City
65.q: Right, so we was so popular in the nightclub scene that - and then we was at the Concord Hotel, was one of the all year around summer resorts, still the best, the biggest in the whole world, forty-five or fifty thousand people; so considering those people live in New York State, during the summer…

26.t: Cootie Williams's hometown Mobile and watermelon
26.s: The Mobile station was packed for Cootie, then the band played a segregated dance.
26.ch: Image, travel and Black, Brown and Beige
26.q: And man, I was sleeping. I heard all this noise, I raised the little shade and saw all these people, I said, man, and everybody's hollering, "Cootie, Cootie." So Cootie come up. He was home, boy. So Duke came out, Duke put on a robe and came to the platform, hollered at us. I ain't never budged. So…

27.s: Phillips says Minneapolis audiences were not segregated, were mostly Black, and the pianist's and drummer's wives were white.
27.q: sure. The piano player, his wife was white, and so was the drummer's wife.

166.t: Segregated dances for Duke and Cab
166.s: Big bands played Black dances at separate Tulsa halls.
166.ch: Family background and the Tulsa music scene
166.q: Sometimes. There was a dance hall there called the Skyline. That was a public dance. Now, when Duke and Cab came to town, Duke would generally play the convention hall, and Cab would be at some arena where they held hockey games, you know. It was an arena, like.

231.t: Performing among whites; black audience seating
231.s: Outside Harlem he was the only black act before mostly white audiences without hassles; black patrons sat scattered in balconies.
231.ch: Porgy and Bess and Varsity Show
231.q: All right, felt all right. I know I wouldn't be there unless I was doing something. I got to be doing something outstanding to be there, man.

89.t: Segregated dances and the three-rope hall
89.s: Black dances had white spectators only, and one Southern hall roped off whites, blacks and mulattos.
89.q: If it was a black dance, there would be white spectators who were not allowed to dance. If it was a white dance, then they didn't have black spectators.

379.t: Breaking the color line; the Beachcomber on Pearl Harbor day
379.s: Latin bands were white, he says; he subs at the Beachcomber on December 7, 1941.
379.q: I said, well, the young generation began to like Machido, because they never heard nothing like that, and they were familiar to them because they were born here, and the sound is familiar to them, and they really (inaudible). So (inaudible) nobody else. The Latin band that was here was a…

28.t: The White Brothers society band, the Bluebirds and the Smart Set
28.s: The light-skinned society elite hired the White Brothers; when they could not play, Butler's Bluebirds played the Smart Set dances, which turned away darker guests, who went to Pythian Hall.
28.q: Now, the White Brothers they were a society band. Zeke ? was playing in that band, Harry White and there were four brothers, Harold White, Edward White, Sparky White, about four, and Zeke was in there, now all those boys, you see, you had to watch Washington during that time. Washington had what…

90.s: Ellington and Lunceford played only white dances in Jackson; at Black dances whites sat in roped-off seating.
90.ch: Touring shows and the bands he heard
90.q: Now, Jimmie Lunceford I wanted to hear. But Jimmie Lunceford and Duke Ellington, the whole time I was at home and could go and hear bands, they never played for the Black dances. Maybe they couldn't afford them or something...

233.t: Playing the Tropicana through the back door
233.s: Before Hamp, he worked a club where black musicians used the back door and sat in a storeroom between sets.
233.q: Before I went with Hamp, I remember working at a place out on the Avenue on 16th Street, at a place called the Tropicana, and we had to come through the back door. There was no blacks in the club, and on our intermission we had to sit in the back room where they had the beer and stuff stored. It…

94.t: Indian audiences in the South and Oklahoma
94.s: Welburn asks about Indian listeners; Moore says Indians are mostly in Oklahoma, where they stared at him playing with Ernie Fields.
94.q: Well, unfortunately, down south you don't find Indians around. The only place you run into Indians is in Oklahoma. There is an all-Indian town there called Pawhuska and Hominy and all the other places. They seen me up there with Ernie Fields, they'd point at me or they whisper among themselves that…

72.t: Mixed audiences and the second balcony
72.s: Black patrons sat in the second balcony, leading Welburn to mention 'Second Balcony Jump'.
72.q: Well, at some places we played it was a mixed audience. But mostly Colored people at... We would sit in the... Not we, but our people(?) used to come in and sit in the back, or either... Some big dance hall or another had what you call a second balcony. Our people had to sit on the second floor.…

149.t: Segregated dances where the crowd tore down the line
149.s: He recalls dances in Rocky Mount and Durham where black and white dancers mixed.
149.q: No. Well, a lot of the places when we played, they had black and white to be there. They may not be sitting They had certain parts for them to be, together. If we were playing a white affair, then they had a place for the blacks. If you're playing blacks, they had a place for the whites.

30.t: Alabama theater where Black audiences were afraid to applaud
30.s: In an Alabama white theater the manager set aside one day for Black patrons, who packed the house and tapped their feet but dared not applaud.
30.q: Yeah. Anyway, we worked everywhere. We went down one -- we had to laugh at that -- we was down in, I think it was Alabama somewhere and played in this theater and it was strictly white, you know. So they decided, the manager decided to give one night to the Negroes. So the night those Negroes -- I…

78.t: Mixed audiences and musicians' role in integration
78.s: The Grand Terrace audience was mixed; Horace says musicians demanded to sit among audiences they entertained, helping break down segregation.
78.ch: Starting out in New York and Chicago
78.q: Things were beginning to change there. (Inaudible) And I really -- I believe you'd agree with me 100 percent -- that the musicianship and the musicians had a lot to do with integration.

171.t: The walkathon band at the Playmore Ballroom
171.s: A four- or five-piece black band played a walkathon at a hall that had admitted only white bands.
171.q: we went to that walk-a-thon. You know what a walk-a-thon is? See, those people who can outlast each other, and they walk so many hours a day.

103.t: Playing in white roadhouse bands before learning about color
103.s: When shows got stranded he sat in with white roadhouse bands and says he did not learn about colored and white until 19 or 20.
103.q: During those periods in different parts and places I've been and always running around, when the show gets stranded in what area - Chattanooga, Louisville, Paducah, or what area - they'd come over and ask me from those roadhouses, you come over and play in this band. I was integrating then. They…
